items.title: Founding & the Four Dynasties of Vijayanagara
items.body:
### The Founding of Vijayanagara (1336 CE)

**In one line:** Vijayanagara ('city of victory') was a great Hindu empire of south India, founded in 1336 on the Tungabhadra river and ruled in turn by four dynasties until 1646.

**Why it is asked:** The founders, the saint who inspired them, the capital's name, and the order of the four dynasties are classic one-mark facts. Define once: a *dynasty* = a ruling family that passes the throne down its own line; *Dravidian* = the south-Indian style of temple building.

**The story**

- In 1336 CE two brothers, **Harihara I and Bukka Raya I**, of the **Sangama** family set up a new kingdom with the blessing of the sage **Saint Vidyaranya**. Tradition names five brothers (Harihara, Bukka, Kampana, Mudappa, Marappa), called **Sangamas** after their father.
- They built their capital at **Hampi** on the **Tungabhadra**, naming it after the local goddess **Pampadevi**. By **1346** they had absorbed the old **Hoysala** kingdom, and the state was also called the **Karnataka kingdom**.
- At its height the empire reached from the **river Krishna in the north to the far south** of the peninsula. Over 300 years four dynasties ruled in turn, the empire peaking under the Tuluvas and declining after the Aravidus.

**Why it matters:** Vijayanagara was the last great Hindu empire of the south and the shield of Deccan Hindu culture against the Deccan Sultanates — a frequent Mains theme on state-building and cultural patronage.

**Picture it**

| Dynasty | Period | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Sangama | 1336–1485 | Founders; Deva Raya II a strong king |
| Saluva | 1485–1505 | Brief; Saluva Narasimha |
| Tuluva | 1505–1570 | Zenith under Krishnadevaraya |
| Aravidu | 1570–1646 | Last line; decline after Talikota |

**Terms explained**
- **Sangama** = the name of the first dynasty, taken from the founders' father.
- **Pampadevi** = the goddess from whose name 'Hampi' is derived.

**Don't confuse:** The **four dynasties** are Sangama → Saluva → Tuluva → Aravidu, in that order; the empire was **founded by the Sangamas (1336)**, not by Krishnadevaraya (who belonged to the later Tuluva line).

**Remember it:** Dynasty order "SSTA" = **S**angama → **S**aluva → **T**uluva → **A**ravidu.

**TL;DR**
- Founded 1336 by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I (Sangama) under Saint Vidyaranya, who is traditionally credited with inspiring its establishment.
- Capital Hampi on the Tungabhadra, named after goddess Pampadevi; also called the Karnataka kingdom.
- Absorbed the Hoysala kingdom by 1346; stretched from the Krishna to the far south.
- Four dynasties: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.
keyPoints: Vijayanagara founded in 1336 CE by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I (Sangama dynasty) under Saint Vidyaranya.
The four dynasties in order: Sangama, Saluva, Tuluva, Aravidu.
Capital Hampi on the Tungabhadra, named after goddess Pampadevi; also called the Karnataka kingdom.
The empire stretched from the river Krishna to the far south of the peninsula.
The Hoysala kingdom was absorbed into Vijayanagara by 1346.

items.title: Krishnadevaraya & the Golden Age of Telugu Literature
items.body:
### Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529)

**In one line:** Krishnadevaraya of the Tuluva dynasty was the greatest Vijayanagara ruler, under whom the empire peaked and Telugu literature reached its 'classic age'.

**Why it is asked:** His dynasty and dates, the title 'Andhra Bhoja', the Ashtadiggajas, and his own book Amuktamalyada are repeatedly tested — and carry a strong AP/Telugu angle. Define once: *Andhra Bhoja* = 'the Bhoja of Andhra', comparing him to King Bhoja, a legendary royal patron of learning.

**The story**

- **Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529)** of the **Tuluva dynasty** took the empire to its **zenith** in land, wealth and culture. **Babur**, in his memoir the **Baburnama**, called him the **most powerful ruler of India**.
- He secured the fertile **Raichur Doab (1520)** from Bijapur and campaigned successfully against the Odisha Gajapatis. He kept **cordial relations with the Portuguese** on the coast and hosted the traveller **Domingo Paes**, who described Hampi's wealth.
- As a builder, he raised a large **dam across the Tungabhadra** with a canal-cum-aqueduct to the capital, and added grand **gopurams** (temple gateway-towers) to Dravidian temples.
- As a patron, his court held the **Ashtadiggajas** — the **eight greatest Telugu poets** — led by **Allasani Peddana** (titled *Andhra Kavita Pitamaha*, 'grandfather of Telugu poetry'). His prime minister was **Timmarusu** and his famous court wit was **Tenali Ramakrishna**. He himself wrote **Amuktamalyada** (Telugu, on statecraft), **Jambavati Kalyanam** (Sanskrit), and **Ushaparinayam** and **Madalasacharita**.

**Why it matters:** His reign is the single most important Vijayanagara topic for AP — the 'golden age' of Telugu letters that still anchors Andhra Pradesh's cultural identity.

**Terms explained**
- **Ashtadiggajas** = literally 'eight elephants of the directions', a metaphor for the eight pillar-poets of the court.
- **Gopuram** = the tall, ornate gateway-tower of a south-Indian temple.

**Don't confuse:** **Amuktamalyada** is Krishnadevaraya's **Telugu** work on polity; **Madhuravijayam** was written by **Gangadevi**, not by him. **Jambavati Kalyanam** is his **Sanskrit** work.

**Remember it:** "Andhra Bhoja = Krishnadevaraya, patron of the eight Telugu 'diggajas'."

**TL;DR**
- Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529, Tuluva) took the empire to its zenith; titled Andhra Bhoja.
- Babur's Baburnama called him the most powerful ruler of India.
- His court's Ashtadiggajas (led by Allasani Peddana) mark the classic era of Telugu literature.
- He authored Amuktamalyada (Telugu, polity) and Jambavati Kalyanam (Sanskrit); built a Tungabhadra dam and won the Raichur Doab (1520).
keyPoints: Krishnadevaraya (r. 1509–1529, Tuluva) took the empire to its zenith; titled Andhra Bhoja.
Babur's Baburnama called him the most powerful ruler of India.
His court's Ashtadiggajas were the eight greatest Telugu poets — the classic era of Telugu literature.
Allasani Peddana (Andhra Kavita Pitamaha) led the Ashtadiggajas; Timmarusu was PM and Tenali Ramakrishna the court poet.
He built a dam and canal-aqueduct across the Tungabhadra and won the Raichur Doab (1520).
He authored Amuktamalyada (Telugu, polity) and Jambavati Kalyanam (Sanskrit).
He had cordial ties with the Portuguese; Domingo Paes visited his court.

items.title: Vijayanagara Administration, Art & Foreign Accounts
items.body:
### How Vijayanagara was governed and remembered

**In one line:** Vijayanagara ran a centralised monarchy through a four-tier territorial system and the nayankara land-grant system, built grand Dravidian temples, and is known to us through foreign travellers' accounts.

**Why it is asked:** The order of the four administrative units, the meaning of *nayankara*, the Hampi temples, and matching travellers to their homelands are all common Prelims items. Define once: *nayankara* = a system of granting land to a military chief (a *nayaka*) in return for keeping soldiers for the king.

**The story**

- Vijayanagara was a **centralised monarchy**: the king held supreme power, helped by a **council of ministers**. The land was divided, from largest to smallest, into **Mandala → Nadu → Sthala → Grama** (province → district → sub-district → village).
- Provinces were held by **nayakas** (military chiefs) under the **nayankara** system — they received land and kept troops ready for the king. At the village level, hereditary officials called **ayagars** ran local affairs.
- Temple building flourished in the **Dravidian** style — the empire's architecture belongs to the south-Indian (Dravidian) tradition. The **Virupaksha** temple (to Shiva as Pampapati) and the **Vittala** temple at Hampi are the icons — the Vittala famous for its **musical pillars** and a **stone chariot**. The era also nurtured **Carnatic music**, **Kuchipudi** dance and **Yakshaganam** theatre.
- Much of what we know comes from **foreign travellers** who admired Hampi's wealth.

**Why it matters:** The nayankara system is a key Mains point on medieval state-building, and the Hampi temples are a staple art-and-culture question (Hampi is a UNESCO World Heritage Site).

**Picture it**

| Traveller | Identity |
|---|---|
| Nicolo de Conti | Italian explorer |
| Abdur Razzaq | Persian ambassador |
| Domingo Paes | Portuguese traveller |
| Fernao Nunes | Portuguese historian |

**Terms explained**
- **Mandala / Nadu / Sthala / Grama** = the four units of government, from the largest region down to the single village.
- **Ayagar** = a hereditary village officer (accountant, headman, etc.).

**Don't confuse:** The hierarchy runs **Mandala (largest) → Nadu → Sthala → Grama (village)** — do not reverse it. **Abdur Razzaq was Persian**, while **Paes and Nunes were Portuguese** and **de Conti Italian**.

**Remember it:** "Nayaka keeps troops for land; village is run by the ayagars."

**TL;DR**
- Administrative hierarchy: Mandala > Nadu > Sthala > Grama.
- Nayankara granted land to military chiefs (nayakas); ayagars were village officers.
- Hampi's Vittala temple is famous for musical pillars and a stone chariot (Dravidian style).
- Key foreign visitors: Nicolo de Conti (Italian), Abdur Razzaq (Persian), Domingo Paes & Fernao Nunes (Portuguese).
keyPoints: Administrative hierarchy: Mandala > Nadu > Sthala > Grama.
The nayankara system granted land to military chiefs (nayakas); ayagars were village functionaries.
Hampi's Vittala temple is famous for musical pillars and a stone chariot (Dravidian style).
Carnatic music, Kuchipudi and Yakshaganam flourished under Vijayanagara.
Key foreign visitors: Nicolo de Conti (Italian), Abdur Razzaq (Persian), Domingo Paes & Fernao Nunes (Portuguese).

items.title: Battle of Talikota (1565) & the Decline
items.body:
### The Battle of Talikota (1565)

**In one line:** At Talikota in 1565 a united front of Deccan Sultanates crushed Vijayanagara, sacked Hampi, and broke the last great Hindu empire of the south.

**Why it is asked:** The year, the Vijayanagara commander, the composition of the winning coalition, and the cause of the long rivalry are the standard test points. Define once: a *doab* = the fertile land lying between two rivers (here the Krishna and Tungabhadra).

**The story**

- The **Battle of Talikota (January 1565)** pitted **Vijayanagara**, led by the aged regent **Aliya Rama Raya** of the Aravidu line, against a **coalition of four Deccan Sultanates** — **Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar and Bidar** — under **Sultan Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur**.
- The coalition won by superior numbers, cavalry and (according to accounts) the defection of Muslim commanders in Vijayanagara's own army. Rama Raya was captured and killed.
- Afterwards, **Hampi was looted and abandoned**. The empire did not vanish at once — it survived feebly under the Aravidus — but it **fragmented**, and power passed to regional **nayakas**.
- The battle was not a bolt from the blue: Vijayanagara and the Bahmani world had fought for **two centuries**, chiefly over the fertile **Raichur doab**, over **war-horse imports** (Arabian/Persian, later via the **Portuguese**), and over trade routes. Rama Raya's meddling in the Sultanates' politics finally united them against him.

**Why it matters:** Talikota is the classic Mains case of a strong state undone by diplomacy and alliance-building — the end of Hindu political power in the Deccan and the rise of the Sultanates.

**Terms explained**
- **Aliya Rama Raya** = the de-facto ruler (regent) of Vijayanagara at Talikota ('Aliya' = son-in-law, of Krishnadevaraya).
- **Raichur doab** = the much-fought-over land between the Krishna and Tungabhadra rivers.

**Don't confuse:** Talikota was **1565**, not 1336 (founding) or 1509 (Krishnadevaraya's accession). The empire **fragmented** after it but limped on under the Aravidus — it did not end on the day of battle.

**Remember it:** "Talikota = 1565, the twin-five that broke Vijayanagara."

**TL;DR**
- Battle of Talikota (1565): Vijayanagara under Aliya Rama Raya was crushed by a Deccan Sultanate coalition.
- The coalition — Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar — was led by Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur.
- Hampi was looted and abandoned; the empire fragmented afterwards.
- The core cause was the two-century rivalry over the Raichur doab, war-horses and trade.
keyPoints: Battle of Talikota (1565): Vijayanagara under Aliya Rama Raya was crushed by a Deccan Sultanate coalition.
The coalition — Bijapur, Golconda, Ahmadnagar, Bidar — was led by Ali Adil Shah of Bijapur.
Hampi was looted and abandoned; the empire fragmented afterwards.
The Raichur doab between the Krishna and Tungabhadra was the core contested region.
War-horse trade (via the Portuguese) and trade routes fuelled the Vijayanagara–Bahmani rivalry.

items.title: Bahmani Kingdom — Founding, Rulers & Mahmud Gawan
items.body:
### The Bahmani Kingdom (1347 CE)

**In one line:** The Bahmani kingdom was the first major Muslim power of the Deccan, founded in 1347, famous for its reforming prime minister Mahmud Gawan.

**Why it is asked:** The founder and his alias, the two capitals, the polyglot Firoz Shah, and Mahmud Gawan's reforms, madrasa and execution are reliable Prelims facts. Define once: a *madrasa* = an Islamic college; *polyglot* = someone who knows many languages.

**The story**

- The kingdom was founded in **1347** by **Alauddin Bahman Shah**, better known as **Hasan Gangu**, an Afghan adventurer who **revolted from the Delhi Sultanate** (declaring independence) as its hold on the Deccan weakened. The first capital was **Gulbarga**.
- **Ahmad Shah Wali (1422–1436)** later shifted the capital to **Bidar**; he was called 'Wali' (the saint) for his link to the Sufi saint **Gesu Daraz**.
- **Firoz Shah Bahmani (1397–1422)** was a learned **polyglot** (Persian, Arabic, Telugu, Kannada, Marathi) who built an **observatory near Daulatabad** and brought **Hindus** into the administration in large numbers.
- The kingdom's most creative phase came under **Muhammad Shah III (1463–1482)**, who came to the throne as a boy with the Iranian-born **Mahmud Gawan** as his guiding minister. Gawan rose from an **Iranian trader** to **Prime Minister**, won Goa, Dabhol, Konkan and Orissa, introduced **revenue reforms**, and built the famous **three-storeyed madrasa at Bidar** that housed 1,000 students. Jealous nobles turned the Sultan against him, and he was **executed in 1481** — a blow from which the kingdom never recovered.

**Why it matters:** Bahmani administration and Gawan's reforms are a core Deccan/AP Mains topic, and the kingdom's break-up created the Sultanates that later shaped Telangana and coastal Andhra.

**Terms explained**
- **Hasan Gangu** = the popular name of the founder, Alauddin Bahman Shah.
- **Gesu Daraz** = the revered Sufi saint of Gulbarga linked to Ahmad Shah Wali.

**Don't confuse:** **Alauddin Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu)** founded the kingdom; **Mahmud Gawan** was the great **minister**, not the founder. Gawan was executed in **1481** (while Muhammad Shah III's reign ended the next year, 1482).

**Remember it:** "Bahmani begins 1347, Gulbarga then Bidar; Gawan reforms then falls (1481)."

**TL;DR**
- Bahmani Kingdom founded in 1347 by Alauddin Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu), an Afghan adventurer.
- Capital shifted Gulbarga → Bidar by Ahmad Shah Wali (linked to Sufi saint Gesu Daraz).
- Firoz Shah Bahmani was a polyglot who built a Daulatabad observatory and included Hindus in administration.
- Mahmud Gawan, an Iranian trader, became PM, reformed revenue, built the Bidar madrasa, and was executed in 1481.
keyPoints: Bahmani Kingdom founded in 1347 by Alauddin Bahman Shah (Hasan Gangu), an Afghan adventurer.
Capital shifted Gulbarga → Bidar by Ahmad Shah Wali (linked to Sufi saint Gesu Daraz).
Firoz Shah Bahmani was a polyglot who built a Daulatabad observatory and included Hindus in administration.
Mahmud Gawan, an Iranian trader, became PM, reformed revenue, and built the Bidar madrasa.
Mahmud Gawan was executed in 1481, accelerating the Bahmani decline.

items.title: Bahmani Administration, Break-up & Deccan Sultanates
items.body:
### Bahmani administration and its break-up

**In one line:** The Bahmani kingdom was run through eight provinces and a divided nobility, and by 1526 it split into five Deccan Sultanates that left a rich Indo-Persian legacy.

**Why it is asked:** The number of tarafs, the Deccani–Afaqi split, the names and dynasties of the five successor Sultanates, and their monuments (Gol Gumbaz, Charminar) are frequently matched in exams. Define once: a *taraf* = a province of the Bahmani kingdom; a *jagir* = land whose revenue was given to a noble instead of a cash salary.

**The story**

- The kingdom was divided into **eight provinces (tarafs)**, each under a **Tarafdar** (major tarafs: Gulbarga, Bidar, Berar, Daulatabad). Nobles were paid in **cash or jagirs**.
- The nobility was permanently split between **Deccanis** (local, Indian-born Muslims) and **Afaqis** or **Pardesis** (newcomers from Iran, Iraq and Central Asia). This **Deccani–Afaqi rivalry** was a constant source of conflict and weakened every reign. The army leaned on the **Amirs** and used **gunpowder** in warfare.
- Weakened by this factionalism, the execution of Mahmud Gawan (1481) and weak later kings, the kingdom **broke up by 1526 into five Deccan Sultanates**.
- These successors were great patrons of **Persian-style architecture** — tall minarets, arches and large domes.

**Why it matters:** The five Sultanates (especially Golconda/Qutub Shahi) directly shaped the history of Telangana and coastal Andhra, making this a key AP-linked topic.

**Picture it**

| Sultanate | Dynasty | Founder |
|---|---|---|
| Bijapur | Adil Shahi | Yusuf Adil Shah |
| Ahmednagar | Nizam Shahi | Malik Ahmad |
| Golconda | Qutub Shahi | Quli Qutub Shah |
| Berar | Imad Shahi | Fatullah Imad Shah |
| Bidar | Barid Shahi | Amir Ali Barid |

**Terms explained**
- **Deccanis vs Afaqis** = the two rival blocs of Bahmani nobles — local-born versus foreign-born Muslims.
- **Dakhini Urdu** = the early southern form of Urdu that grew up under Bahmani rule.

**Bahmani literature (who wrote what)**
- **Dakhini Urdu** became prominent as the local dialect of the Deccan in this period.
- The Sufi saint **Gesu Daraz** of Gulbarga wrote several works in Dakhini Urdu.
- The minister **Mahmud Gawan** authored the Persian works **Riyaz-ul-Insha** (a collection of letters) and **Manazir-ul-Insha** (on the art of letter-writing).

**Don't confuse:** The **Gol Gumbaz** is at **Bijapur** (Adil Shahi — largest dome in Asia), while the **Charminar** is at **Hyderabad** (Qutub Shahi, by Muhammad Quli Qutub Shah) — a very common mismatch trap.

**Remember it:** Five Sultanates "BAGBB" = Bijapur, Ahmednagar, Golconda, Berar, Bidar.

**TL;DR**
- Bahmani kingdom had eight tarafs under Tarafdars; nobles paid in cash or jagirs.
- Nobility split into Deccanis (local) and Afaqis/Pardesis (immigrants); army used gunpowder.
- Broke up by 1526 into five Sultanates: Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmednagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutub Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Bidar (Barid Shahi).
- Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur) has the largest dome in Asia; Charminar built by Muhammad Quli Qutub Shah at Hyderabad; Dakhini Urdu flourished.
keyPoints: Bahmani kingdom had eight tarafs under Tarafdars; nobles paid in cash or jagirs.
Nobility split into Deccanis (local) and Afaqis/Pardesis (immigrants) — a chronic rivalry; army used gunpowder.
Broke up (by 1526) into five Deccan Sultanates: Bijapur (Adil Shahi), Ahmednagar (Nizam Shahi), Golconda (Qutub Shahi), Berar (Imad Shahi), Bidar (Barid Shahi).
Gol Gumbaz (Bijapur) has the largest dome in Asia; Charminar was built by Muhammad Quli Qutub Shah at Hyderabad.
Dakhini Urdu flourished; Gesu Daraz and Mahmud Gawan (Riyaz-ul-Insha) were key writers.
Mahmud Gawan wrote the Persian works Riyaz-ul-Insha and Manazir-ul-Insha; Gesu Daraz wrote in Dakhini Urdu.

items.title: Sangama and Saluva Kings — Reigns, Wars and Writers (1336–1505)
items.body:
### Sangama and Saluva Kings — Reigns, Wars and Writers (1336–1505)

**In one line**
Before Krishnadevaraya, the Sangamas built the empire (Bukka, Harihara II, the two Deva Rayas) and the Saluvas seized it in 1485; exams match these kings to dates, titles, visitors and poets.

**The story**
The brothers began at **Anegondi** and built Vijayanagara across the river. **Bukka I** sent an embassy to **China**; his son **Kumara Kampana** destroyed the **Madurai** Sultanate, a victory his wife **Gangadevi** sang in **Madhuravijayam**. **Harihara II** took imperial titles, and **Sayana** wrote his Vedic commentary. **Deva Raya I** dammed the Tungabhadra, beat Firoz Shah at **Pangal** (1420) and was visited by **Nicolo de Conti**. **Deva Raya II** hired Turkish **archers**, was called **Gajabetekara**, received **Abdur Razzaq** (1443) and honoured **Srinatha**. After weak kings, **Saluva Narasimha** seized power (1485) and patronised **Annamacharya**; the Tuluva regent **Narasa Nayaka** and his son **Vira Narasimha** took over in 1505.

#### Sangama kings and their age

| King / person | Years | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Anegondi** | — | Early seat on the north bank of the Tungabhadra; the city of Vijayanagara rose on the south bank |
| **Harihara I** | 1336–1356 | Founder, with Bukka |
| **Bukka Raya I** | 1356–1377 | Sent an embassy to the Ming court of **China** (1374); fought Bahmani Muhammad Shah I |
| **Kumara Kampana** | c.1371 | Bukka's son; destroyed the **Madurai** Sultanate |
| **Gangadevi** | — | Kampana's wife; wrote the Sanskrit **Madhuravijayam** on the Madurai victory |
| **Harihara II** | 1377–1404 | First to take imperial titles (**Maharajadhiraja**) |
| **Sayana** | 14th c. | Vidyaranya's brother; **Vedarthaprakasha**, the classic commentary on the Vedas |
| **Vidyaranya** | 14th c. | Sringeri pontiff; credited with the **Rajakalanirnaya** (and Panchadasi) |
| **Deva Raya I** | 1406–1422 | Nunes credits him with a Tungabhadra dam and city channel (c.**1410**) |
| **Battle of Pangal** | 1420 | Deva Raya I defeated **Firoz Shah Bahmani** |
| **Nicolo de Conti** | 1420 | Italian; visited under **Deva Raya I** |
| **Deva Raya II** | 1424–1446 | Greatest Sangama king; recruited Turkish/Muslim **archers** |
| **Gajabetekara** | — | Title of Deva Raya II — 'hunter of elephants' |
| **Abdur Razzaq** | 1443 | Persian envoy of the Timurid **Shah Rukh**; came under Deva Raya II |
| **Kumaravyasa** | 15th c. | Kannada Mahabharata (Karnata Bharata Kathamanjari) |
| **Srinatha** | 15th c. | Reddi-court poet honoured with a **kanakabhishekam** at Deva Raya II's court |
| **Mallikarjuna, Virupaksha II, Praudha Raya** | 1446–1485 | Weak kings; **Praudha** Raya (1485) was the last Sangama |

#### Saluva interlude and the Tuluva rise

| Person | Years | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Saluva Narasimha** | 1485–1491 | Chandragiri chief; the **first usurpation** (ended the Sangamas) |
| **Annamacharya** | 1408–1503 | Tallapaka composer of Telugu **sankirtana**s to Venkateswara; patron Saluva Narasimha |
| **Tuluva Narasa Nayaka** | 1491–1503 | **Regent** and real ruler under Narasimha Raya II |
| **Vira Narasimha** | 1505–1509 | Second usurpation (**1505**) — first Tuluva king; elder half-brother of Krishnadevaraya |

**Don't confuse**
- **Deva Raya I** (1406–22: Pangal, Nicolo de Conti) ≠ **Deva Raya II** (1424–46: archers, Gajabetekara, Abdur Razzaq).
- **Madhuravijayam** is by **Gangadevi**, about her husband Kumara Kampana — not by Krishnadevaraya.
- First usurpation = **Saluva Narasimha** (1485); second = **Vira Narasimha** (1505).

**TL;DR**
- Harihara I 1336–56; Bukka I 1356–77 (embassy to China); Harihara II 1377–1404 (Maharajadhiraja).
- Kumara Kampana took Madurai; Gangadevi wrote Madhuravijayam; Sayana wrote the Vedarthaprakasha.
- Deva Raya I: Tungabhadra dam (c.1410), Pangal (1420), Nicolo de Conti.
- Deva Raya II: Muslim archers, Gajabetekara, Abdur Razzaq (1443), Srinatha honoured.
- Saluva Narasimha (1485, first usurpation) patronised Annamacharya; Vira Narasimha (1505) began the Tuluvas.
keyPoints: Kumara Kampana destroyed the Madurai Sultanate; his wife Gangadevi wrote Madhuravijayam.
Sayana, brother of Vidyaranya, wrote the Vedarthaprakasha; Harihara II took the title Maharajadhiraja.
Deva Raya I built a Tungabhadra dam (c.1410), defeated Firoz Shah at Pangal (1420) and was visited by Nicolo de Conti.
Deva Raya II (Gajabetekara) recruited Muslim archers and received Abdur Razzaq in 1443; Srinatha was honoured at his court.
Saluva Narasimha made the first usurpation (1485) and patronised Annamacharya; Vira Narasimha made the second (1505).

items.title: Krishnadevaraya in Detail — Campaigns, Titles, Buildings and the Eight Poets
items.body:
### Krishnadevaraya in Detail — Campaigns, Titles, Buildings and the Eight Poets

**In one line**
Beyond 'Andhra Bhoja' and Amuktamalyada, exams ask which forts he took from the Gajapatis, whom he beat at Raichur, what his other titles meant, and which Ashtadiggaja wrote which book.

**The story**
Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529) first turned east: he took **Udayagiri** (1514) and **Kondavidu** (1515) from the **Gajapati** Prataparudra and raised a **victory pillar** near **Simhachalam**. In **1520** he crushed **Ismail Adil Shah** of Bijapur at **Raichur**. He even restored the Bahmani sultan, earning the title **Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya**, and was hailed as **Mooru Rayara Ganda**. He built **Nagalapura** (Hospet) for his mother and the **Krishna temple** at Hampi for a **Bala Krishna** image from Udayagiri. His **Amuktamalyada**, telling the story of **Andal**, was inspired by Andhra Vishnu of **Srikakulam** and contains the line **'Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa'**. **Purandaradasa** sang in his age; **Barbosa** and **Paes** visited. His minister was **Timmarusu**, and eight poets, the Ashtadiggajas, adorned his court.

#### Campaigns, titles and buildings

| Item | Year | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Udayagiri** | 1514 | Fort (Nellore area) taken from the Gajapatis |
| **Kondavidu** | 1515 | Taken from the **Gajapati** Prataparudra of Odisha |
| **Potnuru–Simhachalam** | c.1516 | Krishnadevaraya set up a **victory pillar** after the Kalinga campaign |
| **Battle of Raichur** | 1520 | Defeated **Ismail Adil Shah** of Bijapur; won the Raichur Doab |
| **Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya** | — | 'Restorer of the Yavana (Muslim) kingdom' — for reinstating Bahmani Mahmud Shah |
| **Mooru Rayara Ganda** | — | 'King of three kings'; also Kannada Rajya Rama Ramana and Andhra Bhoja |
| **Nagalapura** | — | New town (modern **Hospet**) named after his mother Nagala Devi |
| **Krishna temple, Hampi** | 1513 | Built for a **Bala Krishna** image brought from Udayagiri |
| **Amuktamalyada** | — | Story of **Andal** (Goda) and Periyalvar; dedicated to Andhra Vishnu of **Srikakulam** (Krishna district) |
| **Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa** | — | 'Telugu is the finest of the land's languages' — a line of Amuktamalyada |
| **Tirumala statues** | — | Krishnadevaraya with queens **Chinna Devi** and **Tirumala Devi** at the Tirumala temple |
| **Purandaradasa** | 1484–1564 | Pitamaha (father) of **Carnatic** music; Kannada Haridasa |
| **Duarte Barbosa** | c.1516 | Portuguese; praised Vijayanagara's religious **tolerance** |
| **Domingo Paes** | c.1520–22 | Portuguese; described Hampi under **Krishnadevaraya** |

#### The Ashtadiggajas and the minister

| Poet / minister | Work / role | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Allasani Peddana** | **Manucharitramu** | Andhra Kavita Pitamaha; leader of the eight |
| **Nandi Thimmana** | **Parijatapaharanamu** | Nicknamed 'Mukku Thimmana' |
| **Dhurjati** | Sri **Kalahasti**swara Mahatmyamu | Also the Kalahastiswara Satakam |
| **Madayyagari Mallana** | **Rajasekhara** Charitramu | — |
| **Ayyalaraju Ramabhadrudu** | **Ramabhyudayamu** | Also Sakalakatha Sara Sangrahamu |
| **Pingali Surana** | **Kalapurnodayamu** | Also Raghava Pandaviyamu (a double-meaning kavya) |
| **Ramarajabhushanudu (Bhattumurthy)** | **Vasucharitramu** | Named after his later patron Aliya Rama Raya |
| **Tenali Ramakrishna** | **Panduranga** Mahatmyamu | The famous court wit (vikatakavi) |
| **Saluva Timmarusu** | — | Prime minister (Mahapradhana), called '**Appaji**' |

**Don't confuse**
- **Manucharitramu** = Allasani Peddana; **Parijatapaharanamu** = Nandi Thimmana; **Panduranga Mahatmyamu** = Tenali Ramakrishna; **Amuktamalyada** = Krishnadevaraya himself.
- **Srikakulam** of Amuktamalyada is the Andhra Vishnu shrine in Krishna district, not the north-coastal district town.
- The traditional list of eight is not contemporary: Ramarajabhushanudu and Pingali Surana wrote mostly after 1529.

**TL;DR**
- Gajapati war: Udayagiri 1514, Kondavidu 1515, victory pillar near Simhachalam.
- Raichur 1520 — Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur defeated.
- Titles: Andhra Bhoja, Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya, Mooru Rayara Ganda.
- Amuktamalyada — Andal; Srikakulam; 'Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa'.
- Ashtadiggajas: Peddana (Manucharitramu), Thimmana (Parijatapaharanamu), Dhurjati (Kalahasti), Tenali (Panduranga) …; PM Timmarusu (Appaji).
keyPoints: Krishnadevaraya took Udayagiri (1514) and Kondavidu (1515) from the Gajapatis and set up a victory pillar near Simhachalam.
He defeated Ismail Adil Shah of Bijapur at Raichur (1520) and took the title Yavanarajya Sthapanacharya.
Amuktamalyada tells the story of Andal; it was inspired by Andhra Vishnu at Srikakulam and says 'Desa bhashalandu Telugu lessa'.
Ashtadiggajas: Allasani Peddana — Manucharitramu; Nandi Thimmana — Parijatapaharanamu; Dhurjati — Kalahastiswara Mahatmyamu; Tenali Ramakrishna — Panduranga Mahatmyamu.
Saluva Timmarusu ('Appaji') was his prime minister; Purandaradasa, father of Carnatic music, lived in his age.

items.title: After Krishnadevaraya — Achyuta Raya, Talikota in Detail and the Aravidu Dynasty
items.body:
### After Krishnadevaraya — Achyuta Raya, Talikota in Detail and the Aravidu Dynasty

**In one line**
The empire peaked with Krishnadevaraya, wobbled under Achyuta and the puppet Sadasiva, broke at Talikota (1565), and survived another eighty years from Penukonda and Chandragiri under the Aravidus.

**The story**
**Achyuta Deva Raya** built the **Tiruvengalanatha** temple; in his reign **Fernao Nunes** wrote his chronicle and the brothers **Virupanna** and Viranna built the **Lepakshi** temple. **Sadasiva Raya** was a puppet of **Aliya Rama Raya**, Krishnadevaraya's **son-in-law**. On **23 January** 1565 the coalition led by **Ali Adil Shah** I beat him at Talikota (also called **Rakshasi-Tangadi**); **Hussain Nizam Shah** had him beheaded. **Berar** alone **did not join**. Rama Raya's brother **Tirumala** founded the Aravidu line at **Penukonda**; **Venkata II** moved to **Chandragiri**; a nayaka under Venkata III granted **Madras** to the English in **1639**; **Sriranga III** was the last king. **Robert Sewell** later wrote **A Forgotten Empire**.

#### Achyuta Raya and Sadasiva Raya

| King / place | Years | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Achyuta Deva Raya** | 1529–1542 | Successor of Krishnadevaraya; **Tiruvengalanatha** (Achyutaraya) temple, Hampi |
| **Fernao Nunes** | c.1535 | Portuguese horse-trader; chronicle written under **Achyuta** Raya |
| **Lepakshi** | 1530s | Veerabhadra temple (Sri Sathya Sai district, ex-Anantapur) by **Virupanna** and Viranna; hanging pillar, monolithic Nandi |
| **Sadasiva Raya** | 1542–1570 | Puppet king; power with Aliya Rama Raya, Krishnadevaraya's **son-in-law** |

#### Talikota (1565) — who was there

| Person / point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Ali Adil Shah I** (Bijapur) | Leader of the coalition |
| **Hussain Nizam Shah I** (Ahmadnagar) | Had the captured Rama Raya beheaded |
| **Ibrahim Qutb Shah** (Golconda) | Golconda in the coalition |
| **Berar** (Imad Shahi) | The only Sultanate that **did not join** |
| **Rakshasi-Tangadi** | Other name of the battle — two villages near the Krishna |
| **23 January 1565** | Date of the battle |

#### The Aravidu dynasty and after

| King / item | Years | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Tirumala Deva Raya** | 1565–1572 | Founder of the Aravidu line; capital to **Penukonda** |
| **Venkata II** | 1586–1614 | Shifted the capital to **Chandragiri** (later Vellore) |
| **Venkata III** | 1632–1642 | In **1639** the nayaka Damarla Venkatadri granted **Madras** to Francis Day of the English Company |
| **Sriranga III** | 1642–1646 | Last Vijayanagara ruler |
| **Successor states** | 17th c. | Nayakas of **Madurai**, Thanjavur, Gingee, Keladi; Wodeyars of **Mysore** |
| **Robert Sewell** | 1900 | '**A Forgotten Empire**' — translated the chronicles of Paes and Nunes |

**Don't confuse**
- **Ali Adil Shah I** led the coalition; **Hussain Nizam Shah I** killed Rama Raya; **Berar** stayed out. The source PDF's 'Bahmani Sultanate' in the coalition is loose wording — the Bahmanis had already broken up.
- Aravidu capitals: **Penukonda** → **Chandragiri** → Vellore (not back to Hampi).
- **Lepakshi** (Veerabhadra, hanging pillar) is in Andhra Pradesh, not Karnataka.

**TL;DR**
- Achyuta Raya: Tiruvengalanatha temple; Nunes; Lepakshi by Virupanna and Viranna.
- Sadasiva — puppet; Aliya Rama Raya = Krishnadevaraya's son-in-law.
- Talikota/Rakshasi-Tangadi, 23 Jan 1565: led by Ali Adil Shah I; Hussain Nizam Shah beheaded Rama Raya; Berar stayed out.
- Aravidus: Tirumala (Penukonda), Venkata II (Chandragiri), Madras grant 1639, Sriranga III last (1646).
- Robert Sewell — 'A Forgotten Empire' (1900).
keyPoints: Achyuta Deva Raya (1529–42): Tiruvengalanatha temple; Nunes wrote in his reign; Lepakshi temple built by Virupanna and Viranna.
Sadasiva Raya was a puppet of Aliya Rama Raya, Krishnadevaraya's son-in-law.
Talikota (Rakshasi-Tangadi), 23 January 1565: coalition led by Ali Adil Shah I; Hussain Nizam Shah I had Rama Raya beheaded; Berar did not join.
Tirumala Deva Raya founded the Aravidu dynasty at Penukonda; Venkata II moved to Chandragiri; Sriranga III was the last ruler.
Robert Sewell's 'A Forgotten Empire' (1900) translated Paes and Nunes.

items.title: Vijayanagara Administration, Coins and Monuments — the Terms
items.body:
### Vijayanagara Administration, Coins and Monuments — the Terms

**In one line**
The words exams test — amaram, bhandaravada, manya, ayagar, varaha — and the Hampi monuments that set the Vijayanagara style.

**The story**
Under the **nayankara** system a chief held **amaram** land and kept **troops**; he also paid an **annual tribute**. Crown land was **bhandaravada**; tax-free grants were **manya** (to Brahmins, temples as **devadana**, or mathas). In each village **twelve** **ayagar**s, such as the **Karanam** and the **Talari**, were paid in land. The gold **varaha** was the Europeans' **pagoda**; the **pratapa**, **fanam** and **jital** were smaller coins. The army depended on **horses** brought through **Goa**, which **Albuquerque** took in **1510**. Visitors recorded **sati**, and **Methwold** later saw the decline. Hampi, a UNESCO site since **1986**, has the **Virupaksha** temple (Shiva as **Pampapati**), the Vittala temple with its **Garuda** chariot, **raya gopuram**s, **kalyana mandapa**s, the **Lotus Mahal**, the **Elephant Stables**, the **Hazara Rama** royal chapel and the **Mahanavami** Dibba.

#### Administration and land

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Nayankara** | Land assigned to a nayaka who kept **troops** for the king |
| **Amaranayaka / amaram** | Military chief / the land (amaram) he held for service |
| **Nayaka duties** | Paid an **annual tribute**; supplied fixed horses, elephants and foot soldiers |
| **Bhandaravada** | Crown land run directly by the state |
| **Manya** | Tax-free grants — brahmadeya (Brahmins), **devadana** (temples), mathapura (mathas) |
| **Ayagar** | **Twelve** hereditary village servants paid with tax-free land |
| **Karanam, Reddi, Talari** | **Karanam** = accountant; Reddi/Gauda = headman; **Talari** = watchman |

#### Coins, trade and society

| Item | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Varaha** | Gold coin — '**pagoda**' to Europeans, 'hun' in Persian |
| **Pratapa** | Half a varaha |
| **Fanam, tar, jital** | Small coins — **fanam** (gold), tar (silver), **jital** (copper) |
| **Horse trade** | War-**horses** from Arabia and Persia, through the Portuguese at **Goa** |
| **Afonso de Albuquerque** | Took Goa from Bijapur (**1510**); courted Krishnadevaraya |
| **William Methwold** | English merchant (c.1630) — described the decline |
| **Sati** | Described by Nicolo de Conti, Barbosa and Nunes; sati stones (mastikal) survive |

#### Monuments of Hampi

| Monument / term | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Hampi (UNESCO)** | Group of Monuments at Hampi — World Heritage Site since **1986** |
| **Virupaksha temple** | Shiva as **Pampapati**; hall and gopuram added by Krishnadevaraya (1510) |
| **Stone chariot** | In the Vittala temple — a shrine to **Garuda** |
| **Raya gopuram** | Huge royal gateway towers, often taller than the central shrine |
| **Kalyana mandapa** | Pillared hall for the deity's marriage |
| **Lotus Mahal** | In the **Zenana** enclosure; Indo-Islamic arches with Hindu forms |
| **Elephant Stables** | **Eleven** domed chambers |
| **Hazara Rama temple** | **Royal chapel**; Ramayana friezes; early 15th c. (Deva Raya I; older books credit Krishnadevaraya) |
| **Mahanavami Dibba** | "House of Victory" — the king watched the **Mahanavami** festival from it |

**Don't confuse**
- **Amaram** (military land) ≠ **manya** (tax-free religious grant) ≠ **bhandaravada** (crown land).
- **Varaha** (Vijayanagara gold 'pagoda') ≠ **tanka** (Delhi Sultanate silver coin).
- Kakatiya **Nayankara** and **Ayagar** systems were inherited and expanded by Vijayanagara.

**TL;DR**
- Nayankara: amaranayakas hold amaram for troops and tribute; bhandaravada = crown land; manya = tax-free grants (devadana).
- Ayagars: twelve village servants — Karanam, Reddi, Talari.
- Coins: varaha (pagoda/hun), pratapa (½), fanam, jital; horses via Goa (Albuquerque 1510).
- Hampi UNESCO 1986: Virupaksha (Pampapati), Vittala (Garuda chariot), raya gopurams, Lotus Mahal, Hazara Rama, Mahanavami Dibba.
keyPoints: Amaranayakas held amaram land, kept troops and paid an annual tribute; bhandaravada was crown land; manya grants (devadana, brahmadeya) were tax-free.
Twelve ayagars ran each village — the Karanam (accountant), Reddi (headman) and Talari (watchman).
The gold varaha was called 'pagoda' by Europeans; the pratapa was half a varaha.
Hampi became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1986; the Virupaksha temple honours Shiva as Pampapati.
Raya gopurams and kalyana mandapas mark Vijayanagara temples; the Vittala temple's stone chariot is a Garuda shrine.

items.title: Bahmani Sultans in Detail, Mahmud Gawan's Reforms and the Chroniclers
items.body:
### Bahmani Sultans in Detail, Mahmud Gawan's Reforms and the Chroniclers

**In one line**
A ruler-by-ruler view of the Bahmanis (1347–1527), the specific reforms that made Mahmud Gawan famous, and who wrote the histories exams quote.

**The story**
The name may come from the hero **Bahman**; **Ferishta** tells the Gangu legend. Hasan Gangu called Gulbarga **Ahsanabad**. **Muhammad Shah I** won the **Turquoise Throne** from Kapaya Nayaka; **Muhammad Shah II** was **peaceful**. **Firoz Shah** built **Firozabad** on the **Bhima**, beat the Raja of **Kherla**, and **abdicated** for **Ahmad Shah** after Pangal. Ahmad Shah Wali annexed **Warangal** (c.**1425**) and honoured **Gesu Daraz** (**Bande Nawaz**, a **Chishti**). **Humayun** was 'Zalim'; **Muhammad Shah III** came to the throne at **nine**, when the **Russian** **Nikitin** visited. Mahmud Gawan of **Gilan**, the **Khwaja-i-Jahan**, turned **four** tarafs into **eight**, left each governor **one fort**, **measured** land, took **Goa** and **Dabhol**, built his madrasa in **1472**, and fell to a **forged letter**. Power then passed to **Qasim Barid**; **Kalimullah** was the last sultan.

#### Bahmani rulers

| Ruler / point | Years | Fact |
|---|---|---|
| **Origin of the name** | 1347 | From the Persian hero **Bahman** (claimed ancestor); **Ferishta** gives the Brahmin-Gangu story |
| **Gulbarga = Ahsanabad** | 1347 | Hasan Gangu renamed his first capital **Ahsanabad** |
| **Muhammad Shah I** | 1358–1375 | Fought Bukka I and Kapaya Nayaka; won Golconda and the **Turquoise Throne** |
| **Muhammad Shah II** | 1378–1397 | **Peaceful** ruler; built mosques, madrasas and hospitals |
| **Firoz Shah Bahmani** | 1397–1422 | Built **Firozabad** on the **Bhima**; annexed Berar |
| **Kherla** | — | Firoz Shah defeated the Gond Raja Narsing Rai of **Kherla** |
| **Abdication** | 1422 | After Pangal, Firoz Shah **abdicated** for his brother **Ahmad Shah** |
| **Ahmad Shah I Wali** | 1422–1436 | Annexed **Warangal** (c.**1425**); moved the capital to Bidar |
| **Gesu Daraz** | d.1422 | **Khwaja Bande Nawaz**, a **Chishti** saint; dargah at Gulbarga; Dakhini writer |
| **Humayun Shah** | 1458–1461 | Called '**Zalim**' (the Cruel); appointed Mahmud Gawan a minister |
| **Muhammad Shah III** | 1463–1482 | Became sultan at **nine**; Mahmud Gawan regent |
| **Athanasius Nikitin** | c.1469–72 | **Russian** merchant from Tver; described Bidar under Muhammad Shah III |
| **Qasim Barid** | after 1482 | Minister holding real power; father of the Barid Shahi line |
| **Kalimullah Shah** | to 1527 | Last Bahmani sultan |

#### Mahmud Gawan's reforms

| Reform / point | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Origin** | From **Gilan** in Persia; came as a merchant |
| **Khwaja-i-Jahan** | His title as chief minister |
| **Tarafs split** | The **four** big tarafs became **eight**, to curb governors |
| **Forts** | Each tarafdar kept only **one fort**; others under central commanders |
| **Revenue** | Land **measured** to fix the revenue demand |
| **Conquests** | **Goa** and **Dabhol** (sea trade with Iran and Iraq); also Konkan and Orissa campaigns |
| **Bidar madrasa** | Built **1472**; three storeys; about 1,000 students |
| **Execution (1481)** | A **forged letter** planted by rival (Deccani) nobles |

#### Chroniclers and writings

| Work / writer | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Ferishta** | Tarikh-i-Ferishta (Gulshan-i-Ibrahimi), written at Bijapur under **Ibrahim Adil Shah II** |
| **Burhan-i-Maasir** | By Sayyid Ali Tabatabai — Bahmani and Nizam Shahi chronicle |
| **Manazir-ul-Insha** | Mahmud Gawan's Persian manual on **letter-writing** |

**Don't confuse**
- The source PDF says Ahmad Shah 'defeated the Kakatiya ruler' at Warangal — the Kakatiyas had fallen in 1323; he annexed Warangal from their successors.
- **Gawan** was executed in **1481** (the PDF says 1482, the end of Muhammad Shah III's reign).
- **Athanasius Nikitin** (Russian) visited the **Bahmanis**; **Abdur Razzaq** (Persian) visited **Vijayanagara**.

**TL;DR**
- Muhammad Shah I — Turquoise Throne; Firoz Shah — Firozabad on the Bhima; Ahmad Shah Wali — Warangal (c.1425).
- Gesu Daraz = Bande Nawaz (Chishti, Gulbarga); Humayun 'Zalim'.
- Nikitin (Russian, Tver) visited c.1469–72.
- Gawan (Gilan, Khwaja-i-Jahan): 4 → 8 tarafs, one fort per tarafdar, land measured, Goa & Dabhol, madrasa 1472, forged letter.
- Ferishta wrote under Ibrahim Adil Shah II; Kalimullah was the last sultan.
keyPoints: Muhammad Shah I won Golconda and the Turquoise Throne from Kapaya Nayaka.
Firoz Shah built Firozabad on the Bhima and abdicated for Ahmad Shah after Pangal; Ahmad Shah Wali annexed Warangal (c.1425).
Gesu Daraz, also called Khwaja Bande Nawaz, was a Chishti saint of Gulbarga.
The Russian merchant Athanasius Nikitin visited the Bahmani kingdom c.1469–72.
Mahmud Gawan (Khwaja-i-Jahan) split four tarafs into eight, left each tarafdar one fort, measured land, and was executed on a forged letter.
Ferishta wrote the Tarikh-i-Ferishta at Bijapur under Ibrahim Adil Shah II.

Mahmud Gawan's reforms: he divided the four tarafs (provinces) into eight, allowed each tarafdar to keep only one fort under his direct control (the rest went to royal officers), and had land measured to fix the revenue demand.

items.title: The Five Deccan Sultanates — Founders, Dates, Ends and Monuments
items.body:
### The Five Deccan Sultanates — Founders, Dates, Ends and Monuments

**In one line**
Five kingdoms grew out of the Bahmani state between 1489 and 1528 and fell one by one — two to each other and three to the Mughals; exams match founders, dates, annexations and monuments.

**The story**
**Yusuf Adil Shah** founded Bijapur in **1489**; **Malik Ahmad** founded Ahmadnagar and **Fathullah** Imad-ul-Mulk founded Berar (capital **Ellichpur**) in **1490**; **Sultan Quli** founded Golconda in **1518**; **Amir Ali Barid** made Bidar independent. By about **1526** the Bahmani state was gone. **Berar**, the **shortest**-lived, fell to Ahmadnagar (**1574**); Bidar fell to Bijapur (**1619**); **Shah Jahan** took Ahmadnagar (**1636**) despite the earlier resistance of **Chand Bibi** and **Malik Ambar**, an **Abyssinian**; Aurangzeb took Bijapur (**1686**) and Golconda (**1687**). Bijapur's **Ibrahim Adil Shah I** made **Hindvi** official; **Ibrahim Adil Shah II** ('**Jagadguru**') wrote the **Kitab-i-Nauras** and lies in **Ibrahim Rauza**. The **Gol Gumbaz** has a **whispering gallery**. Gulbarga has the **Jama Masjid** and **Haft Gumbaz**; Bidar has the **Solah Khamba** mosque and gives its name to **Bidriware**.

#### Founders

| Sultanate | Founder, year | Annexed by |
|---|---|---|
| **Bijapur** (Adil Shahi) | **Yusuf Adil Shah**, **1489** | Aurangzeb, 1686 |
| **Ahmadnagar** (Nizam Shahi) | **Malik Ahmad** Bahri, **1490** | Shah Jahan, 1633–36 |
| **Berar** (Imad Shahi) | **Fathullah** Imad-ul-Mulk, 1490; capital **Ellichpur** | Ahmadnagar, 1574 |
| **Golconda** (Qutb Shahi) | **Sultan Quli** Qutb-ul-Mulk, **1518** | Aurangzeb, 1687 |
| **Bidar** (Barid Shahi) | **Amir Ali Barid**, independent 1528 (PDF: 1518) | Bijapur, 1619 |

#### Break-up and annexation

| Event | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Break-up** | By about **1526** the five Sultanates were independent |
| **End of Berar** | **Shortest**-lived; annexed by Ahmadnagar in **1574** (PDF: 1572) |
| **End of Bidar** | Annexed by Bijapur in **1619**; the Mughals took the fort in 1656–57 |
| **End of Ahmadnagar** | Annexed by **Shah Jahan** (1633–**1636**) |
| **End of Bijapur** | Annexed by Aurangzeb in **1686** |
| **End of Golconda** | Annexed by Aurangzeb in **1687** |

#### People and monuments

| Person / monument | Fact |
|---|---|
| **Chand Bibi** | Defended Ahmadnagar against **Akbar**'s army (1595–1600) |
| **Malik Ambar** | **Abyssinian** minister of Ahmadnagar; guerrilla war on the Mughals; land-revenue settlement |
| **Ibrahim Adil Shah I** | Made **Hindvi** (Dakhini) the official language instead of Persian |
| **Ibrahim Adil Shah II** | Called '**Jagadguru**'; wrote the **Kitab-i-Nauras** (songs in Dakhini) |
| **Gol Gumbaz** | Tomb of Muhammad Adil Shah (1656); huge dome with a **whispering gallery** |
| **Ibrahim Rauza** | Tomb of Ibrahim Adil Shah II at Bijapur (said to have inspired the Taj Mahal) |
| **Bara Kaman** | Unfinished tomb of Ali Adil Shah II |
| **Jama Masjid, Gulbarga** | 1367; the whole courtyard is **roofed** with domes |
| **Haft Gumbaz** | Seven-domed Bahmani royal tombs at Gulbarga |
| **Rangeen Mahal, Solah Khamba** | Palace and sixteen-pillared mosque at Bidar |
| **Bidriware** | Silver inlay on blackened zinc alloy; named after Bidar (GI tag) |

**Don't confuse**
- **Gol Gumbaz** (Muhammad Adil Shah) ≠ **Ibrahim Rauza** (Ibrahim Adil Shah II) — both at Bijapur. 'Taj of the Deccan' is the Mughal Bibi-ka-Maqbara at Aurangabad.
- The PDF's 'largest dome in Asia' for Gol Gumbaz is a popular claim; standard books call it one of the largest domes in the world.
- **Chand Bibi** fought **Akbar**; **Malik Ambar** fought **Jahangir**'s armies.

**TL;DR**
- Founders: Bijapur 1489 (Yusuf Adil Shah), Ahmadnagar 1490 (Malik Ahmad), Berar 1490 (Fathullah, Ellichpur), Golconda 1518 (Sultan Quli), Bidar (Amir Ali Barid).
- Ends: Berar 1574 (Ahmadnagar), Bidar 1619 (Bijapur), Ahmadnagar 1636 (Shah Jahan), Bijapur 1686, Golconda 1687 (Aurangzeb).
- Chand Bibi vs Akbar; Malik Ambar (Abyssinian) vs the Mughals.
- Ibrahim Adil Shah II — Jagadguru, Kitab-i-Nauras; Gol Gumbaz — whispering gallery; Bidriware from Bidar.
keyPoints: Yusuf Adil Shah founded Bijapur (1489); Malik Ahmad founded Ahmadnagar (1490); Sultan Quli founded Golconda (1518); Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk founded Berar with its capital at Ellichpur.
Berar, the shortest-lived Sultanate, fell to Ahmadnagar in 1574; Bidar fell to Bijapur in 1619.
Shah Jahan annexed Ahmadnagar (1636); Aurangzeb annexed Bijapur (1686) and Golconda (1687).
Chand Bibi defended Ahmadnagar against Akbar; Malik Ambar, an Abyssinian, fought the Mughals.
Ibrahim Adil Shah II was called 'Jagadguru' and wrote the Kitab-i-Nauras; Gol Gumbaz has a whispering gallery.

items.title: For Mains — Vijayanagara & the Bahmani Kingdom
items.body:
## For Mains — Vijayanagara & the Bahmani Kingdom (Paper-II, clause M2-2b)

Mains in Paper-II treats these two states together as the shapers of the medieval Deccan and of Telugu culture. Build answers around the comparison and the AP angle, not a date-list.

| Dimension | Vijayanagara | Bahmani / Deccan Sultanates |
|---|---|---|
| Polity | Centralised Hindu monarchy; nayankara land-grant system; Mandala–Nadu–Sthala–Grama | Islamic sultanate; eight tarafs; Deccani vs Afaqi nobility |
| Economy | Agrarian prosperity, coastal trade, war-horse imports via the Portuguese | Revenue reforms under Mahmud Gawan; Konkan/Goa trade |
| Culture | Dravidian temples (Hampi), Carnatic music, 'classic age' of Telugu (Ashtadiggajas) | Indo-Persian architecture, Dakhini Urdu, Sufism (Gesu Daraz) |
| Decline | Talikota (1565), Hampi sacked, power to nayakas | Deccani–Afaqi feud, Gawan's execution (1481), split into five Sultanates by 1526 |

**Data points and authorities to quote:** founding 1336 (Harihara–Bukka, Vidyaranya) and 1347 (Hasan Gangu); Krishnadevaraya's *Amuktamalyada* and the Ashtadiggajas led by Allasani Peddana; foreign accounts of Abdur Razzaq, Domingo Paes and Fernao Nunes; Mahmud Gawan's Bidar madrasa and his execution in 1481; Talikota 1565; the five successor Sultanates (Adil, Nizam, Qutub, Imad, Barid Shahi).

**Use in answers:**
- *Example:* contrast Vijayanagara's nayankara system with the Bahmani taraf system to show two different answers to the same problem — holding a large Deccan state together.
- *Quote:* Babur's Baburnama describing Krishnadevaraya as the most powerful ruler of India.
- *Diagram idea:* a Deccan map marking Hampi, Gulbarga/Bidar and the Raichur doab to show why the two powers kept colliding.
- *AP link:* the Qutub Shahis of Golconda (a Bahmani successor) and the 'classic age' of Telugu under Krishnadevaraya are both central to Andhra Pradesh's heritage — the strongest AP angle in medieval history.
keyPoints: Frame the answer as a comparison of two Deccan state models — Vijayanagara's nayankara monarchy vs the Bahmani taraf sultanate.
Cultural high points to cite: Hampi's Dravidian temples and the 'classic age' of Telugu (Ashtadiggajas) vs Indo-Persian architecture and Dakhini Urdu.
Key dates/data: 1336, 1347, Raichur Doab (1520), Mahmud Gawan executed 1481, Talikota 1565, five Sultanates by 1526.
Decline contrast: Vijayanagara fell by military defeat (Talikota), the Bahmanis by internal factionalism (Deccani–Afaqi).
AP angle: Krishnadevaraya's Telugu golden age and the Qutub Shahis of Golconda are central to Andhra Pradesh's heritage.
